title: COP31 ended in collapse. What does it mean for the Philippines?
summary: Officially the longest climate negotiation on record, COP31 ended in collapse on Monday morning (Manila time) after nations failed to agree on a cover decision or what they call the Antalya Pact.

blocks.text: COP31 officially became the longest climate negotiations on record after it spilled two days into overtime.
But those extra 48 hours weren't enough to get nations to agree on a cover decision, or what was being dubbed the Antalya Pact.

The negotiations ended in collapse on Monday morning (Manila time) with nations like Pakistan, Indonesia, Azerbaijan, China, and Saudi Arabia supporting the cover decision, while nations like the European Union walking away.

The EU could not support the deal because there was no mention of fossil fuels, essentially the cause of climate change, while Panama "said the pact weakened previously agreed decisions and failed to reflect the urgency of keeping the 1.5°C goal within reach," the UN reported. Meanwhile, the Marshall Islands warned the "deal failed countries on the front lines of climate change.
Together with several nations including Fiji, Russia, Nepal, Singapore, and Mexico, the Philippines wasn't clear in its position about the cover decision.
A Word of Caution

Speaking at a virtual post-COP press briefing organized by Aksyon Klima Pilipinas, WWF’s Climate and Energy Program Head Atty. Angela Ibay advised to "caution ourselves in labeling [COP31] as 'a failure'."
Pointing to her experience of attending the global negotiations since COP 3, Ibay clarified it isn't really a standard that each COP should have a cover decision."
"Too much time was spent with the proposed cover decision showing minor progress," she said.

It's a point that Ellenor Bartolome of the Philippine Movement for Climate Justice agrees to. "The focus has been too much on the cover decision that has strained and distracted us from the negotiating tracks that were supposed to secure concrete outcomes to move things forward," Bartolome said in the same briefing.

"The clear baseline, the mechanism and other plans to triple adaptation finance remain empty. The funds for loss and damage are running dry. Mitigation work program failed to reach consensus," she continued, adding developing countries like the Philippines needed COP31 to respond to climate emergencies already taking place. "Instead, it responded with delay, detours, and denials to finance."
Points of Contention

The EU walked away from the deal because "fossil fuel" was not in the proposed cover decision. But ahead of COP31, EU climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said fresh climate finance pledges were "dead in the water."
According to Ibay, two big reasons why things fell apart at COP31 were the "discussion on transitioning away from fossil fuels" and "a lot of discussion on finance."
"As always, there was too little of what was needed," Ibay said.

On Wednesday's Sayang Ang Araw forum organized by FYT.PH, Rep. Anna Veloso-Tuazon, house committee on climate change, emphasized what developing nations have long been asking in these climate negotiations: "Where is the finance?"
Present in Antalya for COP31, Tuazon shared "we started COP31 with a dialogue on transitioning away from fossil fuels."
"But like many of G77 and like-minded countries, we can't just pay lip service to transitioning away from it without the means of implementation," she said.
"We want to be able to reduce emissions but we need the funding. We need the tech transfers. We need capacity building to make it happen," Tuazon continued.

Added Bartolome, "the finance and the support to survive, alongside Just Transition and resilience-building, must arrive as fast as the warming does. These should've been central to the negotiations and outcomes but it ended with nothing to show for the Global South."

"This is a climate justice issue," Tuazon reminds. "If those who are historically responsible are asking us to commit to transition away from fossil fuel right now, without out giving us the means to make it happen, it's going to be very difficult for our development," Tuazon continued.
"Climate finance is still very crucial to making this happen and this is why we walked away from COP31 with disappointment."
Other Important Things for the Philippines

Among many things, the failed deal had included the 35x35 global electrification push which the Philippines supported; it had acknowledged the planet’s temperature overshoot, which Tuazon calls is an important gain from the negotiations; and according to WWF’s Climate and Energy Program Head Atty. Angela Ibay, the cover decision had also “for the first time acknowledged the importance of our oceans.”
“For a country like the Philippines that is archipelagic, the ocean dialogues and the issues around it is quite important," Ibay said at Tuesday's post-COP virtual press briefing.
"If we had had a cover decision, that would have been a very welcome centerpiece for us to latch on for many of the work that we’re doing in the Philippines," Ibay said.

Reiterating that "the cover decision is not required," Ibay admits the cover decision does set the political code, providing "signals for countries to move forward with their plans, whether its to the NDCs, to their national adaptation plans, and to see whether climate finance will flow directly to those who really need it."

At COP 31, the Philippines launched and presented a number of these national plans including our updated NDCs, our Just Transition Framework, the Philippine Carbon Market Policy Framework, and the Philippine Climate Finance Strategy.

Said John Leo Algo, national coordinator of Aksyon Klima Pilipinas, the lack of a cover decision "may also be a sign for the country to be more aggressive in making developed countries live up to their word, especially during the closing plenary of COP31, on being 1.5°C-aligned."
"It is impossible to be 1.5°C-aligned without the provision of finance," he said.

Meanwhile, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources in a statement emphasized "that climate finance must be measured not only by the amount pledged or mobilized, but also whether it is delivered in a timely, adequate, and accessible manner and reaches the countries and communities that need it most."

“Ultimately, climate finance must enable vulnerable communities not only to withstand climate impacts, but also to protect their livelihoods, rebuild where necessary, and secure a future where they can thrive,” DENR Sec. Juan Miguel Cuna said.
"There is still work to be done to be able to move forward," Ibay said. "We still need to continue fighting for our communities, for our cities, and for our country itself." — GMA News
